title: A pricing page for an accounting firm
metaTitle: Accounting firm pricing page that shows fit
excerpt: An accounting firm pricing page should show the fee shape, what is included, and how to book a call. Founders use it to judge fit, not to do arithmetic.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper, a map of decisions in the way a pricing page should show the shape of a fee.
caption: A flow sketched by hand, with the user's goal written on the page. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should an accounting firm publish its fees?
faqs.answer: Publish the shape even when a single number would mislead. Monthly closes, annual returns, cleanups, and advisory retainers are different fits. Print a dollar figure when you will honor it, and publish the variables when the year is what changes the fee.

faqs.question: What belongs in the included and excluded lists?
faqs.answer: Name the reports, the reviews, and the filing steps the fee actually covers, and name who signs the work. Say what is left out, such as catch-up bookkeeping on a return-only fee, or a second entity. The excluded list is what makes the included list believable.

faqs.question: How should the pricing page ask people to start?
faqs.answer: Ask them to book a call once the shape is visible, and tell them what to know beforehand. Entity type, how the records are kept, and the question they want answered are enough. The call should confirm fit. It should not be a surprise invoice or a free year-end.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A founder who needs a calm expert uses an accounting firm pricing page to judge fit. They want the shape of the fee, what the shape includes, and how to book a call. They are not there to do arithmetic on a year they have not described yet. If every intro call starts with "so how do you charge," the page should have answered with the shape already.

Nielsen Norman Group found that people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on pages they open, and that they often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. The shape has to be the part they cannot miss. Google's helpful-content guidance warns against pages that send someone back to search to finish the job. A fee page that only says "contact us for a tailored proposal" is one of those pages, especially on a topic that touches financial stability, where trust is the point.

## Fit, before the total

The founder is deciding whether your way of working matches the mess or the rhythm they actually have.

A company with a bookkeeper in the office may only need the annual accounts and the return. A founder who has been in the product and not in the ledger may need a cleanup before any monthly rhythm makes sense. A clinic that wants a number every month is buying a close, not a speech. A studio heading into a raise may need a defined project to make the books legible to someone else. Those are different shapes. A single "packages from" line flattens them, and the founder cannot tell which box they are in.

Write the page so they can sort in a minute. Name the ways you actually charge. Say which way you will only scope after a call. Put "book a call" where the distinction is already visible, so the booking is a confirmation of fit, not a hunt for the price.

Calm, here, is the absence of a trick. No teaser that becomes a different fee once they are on the phone. No excellence banner where the scope should be. The tone can be quiet because the lists are complete.

## The shapes a founder can picture

Publish the shape even when the dollar figure depends on the year.

- A monthly fee for a defined close. Say what "defined" means. Bank recs, a set of reports, a short call, questions answered within an agreed window.
- A fixed fee for the annual accounts and the return, once the books are current. Say what "current" means, or the fixed fee is a fiction.
- A cleanup project, priced as a range or as phases, for a ledger that has gone quiet. The first phase might be seeing how far behind things are. The second phase is the catch-up. Do not pretend you know the second phase from a logo.
- A retainer for a known advisory rhythm, such as a quarterly cash review, separate from compliance so nobody thinks the return includes a shadow CFO.
- Hourly work for the questions that fall outside those shapes, with the kinds of questions that usually land there.

Match shapes to the companies you named on the homepage. Product companies, clinics, shops, studios, trades. If a shop with inventory is priced differently from a services firm because of stock, say that in one sentence. The variable is part of the fit.

Write the number when it is stable and you will honor it. A monthly fee that is real lets a founder compare you with the cost of staying confused. If the number moves, publish the variables. Months behind. Number of accounts. Payroll complexity. Inventory. Whether the records are in a ledger or in a folder of exports. Multi-entity groups.

Do not publish a number you hope to negotiate up. Founders who need calm experts remember the first number. Google's emphasis on trust for financial topics is a reason to let the page and the call say the same shape.

## Included, and not included

Each shape needs two lists, in the founder's words.

Included, for a monthly close, might be the reconciliations you name, the reports you name, and one working session. Included, for a return, might be the preparation, the review with them, and the filing steps you actually perform. Say who signs what. If a licensed person reviews before filing, that belongs in the included list, because it is the reason they hired a firm and not only a piece of software.

Left out might be bookkeeping when they bought only the return, legal work, chasing their customers, rebuilding a year with no records, or a second entity. The excluded list is what makes the included list believable. A founder who has been surprised by an accountant before is reading for the surprise. Name it.

Disbursements and software fees, if they pass through, sit in the same view as the fee. A filing fee hidden in a footer is a small betrayal on a page about money. Say it in the same size type as the shape.

If a cleanup can expand, say the checkpoint. "After we see the first month, we confirm the rest of the project before more work starts." That sentence is calm. An open-ended "it depends" with no checkpoint is how a founder imagines an invoice they cannot predict.

## Book the call after the shape is clear

The action is to book a call, and the page should say what makes the call useful.

Ask them to know, even roughly, the entity type, how the records are kept, and the question they want answered. Last year's return helps if they have it. They do not need a perfect management pack to earn the conversation. A ten-field form between a clear fee and a human is how you lose the founder who was ready.

Say what you will confirm on the call. Which shape applies. What you would need in the first month. Whether you are the right firm for their kind of company. The call is a fit check. It is not a free year-end, and it is not a software demo unless you truly sell software, in which case this is the wrong page.

Use the same words as the button on the homepage. Book a call. If the calendar is the next step, the button can open it, with the duration written beside it. If a person still has to accept the booking, say that. A founder will forgive a short wait they were told about. They will not forgive a calendar that looked confirmed and was not.

## Make the quarter they read be the right quarter

Because only about a quarter of the text gets read, do not bury the shape under a story about your values.

Give each offer a heading a founder would say. "Monthly books." "Annual return, if the ledger is current." "Cleanup before a raise or a loan." Put the shape in the first sentence. Put the lists next. Put the booking at the top of the page and again after the offer they care about.

Skip a matrix where every cell says bespoke or tailored. That grid is the word excellence in table form. Two or three shapes, written fully, are enough. The services page can explain the work. This page explains the money. They should not contradict each other. If the services page promises management accounts inside the monthly fee, the pricing page has to say the same thing.

A calculator is rarely calm. Revenue times a magic ratio is not a quote. Use a calculator only for a defined add-on you can actually compute, such as a known payroll tier, and label it as that. Otherwise the variables belong in sentences.

## What this page should refuse

A "from" price that is only the cheapest entity and the lightest month. If most founders you want would not qualify, do not lead with it.

A skyline, a glass lobby, or a paragraph of excellence above the lists. The founder came to see if the relationship fits the year they are having.

A promise of a tax outcome. "We always reduce your bill" is a claim you should not print. You can say you will explain the position and file what is supportable. That is the calm version, and it is the one you can keep.

A bundled pile that forces a monthly CFO onto a founder who needed a return. Unbundle the shapes so they can buy the one that fits. You can say what usually comes next without making it mandatory in the first month.

Jokes about shoeboxes and receipts. Some founders are behind. Shaming them on the pricing page is the opposite of calm. Describe the cleanup as a phase with a checkpoint. Dignity is part of the fit.

## When the year is too messy for a public number

Say that plainly, then price the part you can see. A paid look at the ledger, a fixed first month, or a short diagnostic call that ends with a written shape. The founder should leave the page knowing there is a door, and knowing the door is not a blank invoice.

Do not use the mess as a reason to hide the shapes you do know. Monthly books for a current ledger can still have a shape beside the sentence about cleanups. Hiding everything because some years are hard punishes the founder who is organized.

Once the shapes are honest, the services themselves still have to be written as jobs. A fee attached to "advisory" is hard to trust. Read [what the services page needs to say](/blog/the-services-page-an-accounting-firm-actually-needs) so each offer has an outcome, a boundary, and a way to book.

When you want a second pair of eyes on whether the fee is understandable, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the three shapes you are asked about every week.
